body:
Rewrite this SQL query for better performance:

SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (
  SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE registration_date > '2023-01-01'
)
answer:
Rewrite with a JOIN (or EXISTS) and select only the needed columns:

SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.order_date, o.total_amount
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE c.registration_date > '2023-01-01';

Or with EXISTS:

SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.order_date, o.total_amount
FROM orders o
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM customers c
  WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id AND c.registration_date > '2023-01-01'
);

Why it is faster:
• The optimizer can use an efficient join strategy (hash/merge/nested-loop with indexes) instead of building and probing the IN-list; EXISTS stops at the first match.
• Selecting named columns instead of * reads and transfers less data and allows covering indexes.
• Supporting indexes: customers(registration_date, customer_id) and orders(customer_id).
(customer_id is the primary key of customers, so the join cannot duplicate orders.)
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• A correct rewrite using JOIN or EXISTS that returns the same orders — 3 marks.
• Replacing SELECT * with specific columns — 1 mark.
• Explanation of why it performs better and/or suggestion of supporting indexes on customers.registration_date and orders.customer_id — 2 marks.
• Column names other than customer_id/registration_date are illustrative; accept any sensible order columns.
hint: Two things slow it down: SELECT * and the IN (subquery). Think JOIN or EXISTS, and only the columns you need.

body:
Explain how indexing improves the query:

SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (
  SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE registration_date > '2023-01-01'
)
answer:
An index is a sorted data structure (usually a B-tree) holding column values with pointers to their rows, so the DBMS can find matching rows without scanning the whole table.

For this query:
• Index on customers(registration_date): the range condition registration_date > '2023-01-01' becomes an index range seek instead of a full scan of customers. A composite index (registration_date, customer_id) "covers" the subquery, so the table itself need not be read.
• Index on orders(customer_id): for each qualifying customer the DBMS seeks straight to that customer's orders instead of scanning every order row; it also enables efficient join strategies.

Benefits: far fewer disk pages read (lower I/O), faster response time, less CPU, and better scalability as tables grow — search time grows roughly logarithmically instead of linearly.

Trade-off: indexes take storage and slow down INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE slightly because they must be maintained, so index the columns used in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY.
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• What an index is / how it works (sorted structure, B-tree, pointers, avoids full scans) — 2 marks.
• Applied to this query: index on registration_date for the filter — 1.5 marks; index on orders.customer_id for the lookup/join — 1.5 marks.
• Benefit or trade-off discussed (less I/O, faster; maintenance cost on writes) — 1 mark.
hint: An index is like a book's index: instead of reading every page (full table scan), jump straight to the rows. Which columns are searched and joined here?

body: What is a query execution plan? How can it help in optimizing queries?
answer:
A query execution plan is the sequence of operations the DBMS's query optimizer chooses to execute a SQL statement — which tables to access, whether to use an index seek or a full table scan, the join order and join algorithm (nested loop, hash, merge), sorts, aggregations — along with estimated (or actual) rows and costs for each step. It is viewed with EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE (MySQL, PostgreSQL) or "Display Execution Plan" (SQL Server).

How it helps optimization:
• Reveals full table scans where an index seek was expected, showing which indexes to create.
• Shows inefficient join order or join types and expensive operations such as large sorts, temporary tables or key lookups.
• Compares estimated and actual row counts, exposing stale statistics that mislead the optimizer.
• Shows whether a rewrite (e.g. IN → JOIN/EXISTS, removing functions on indexed columns, avoiding SELECT *) actually reduced cost.
• Lets you measure the effect of each change before deploying it.
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• Definition: the optimizer's chosen steps/strategy for executing a query (access paths, joins, costs) — 2 marks; mention of EXPLAIN or equivalent is a plus.
• How it helps: at least two concrete uses (identify table scans/missing indexes, join order/type, costly sorts, statistics, compare rewrites) — 4 marks.
hint: It's the DBMS's step-by-step recipe for running your SQL. What can you spot in that recipe that is slow?

body: Compare NoSQL databases with traditional RDBMS. Provide use cases for each.
answer:
RDBMS (e.g. MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server):
• Data model: tables of rows and columns with relationships (foreign keys).
• Schema: fixed, defined in advance.
• Query language: SQL, with powerful joins.
• Consistency: ACID transactions; strong consistency.
• Scaling: mainly vertical (bigger server); horizontal scaling is harder.
Use cases: banking and financial transactions, ERP, payroll, inventory and order processing, student records — anywhere integrity and complex queries matter.

NoSQL (e.g. MongoDB, Cassandra, Redis, Neo4j):
• Data models: document, key-value, wide-column, graph.
• Schema: flexible/schema-less.
• Query: database-specific APIs; joins limited.
• Consistency: often BASE / eventual consistency (tunable), trading consistency for availability and partition tolerance.
• Scaling: horizontal, sharding across many commodity servers; high write throughput.
Use cases: social media feeds and user profiles (document), caching and sessions (Redis key-value), IoT/time-series and big-data logging (Cassandra), recommendation engines and fraud networks (graph), content management with varying structure.
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• Valid comparison points (data model, schema, scalability, consistency/ACID vs BASE, query language) — up to 4 marks, ~1 per well-explained contrast.
• At least one appropriate use case for RDBMS — 1 mark; for NoSQL — 1 mark.
hint: Compare data model, schema, scaling, consistency and query language — then give a fitting application for each.

body: What are the challenges in managing distributed databases? Mention at least 4.
answer:
1. Data consistency and replication: keeping replicas synchronised; conflicts when the same data is updated at different sites; CAP trade-off between consistency and availability.
2. Distributed transaction management and concurrency control: ensuring atomicity across sites needs protocols like two-phase commit, which are slow and can block; distributed deadlocks are hard to detect.
3. Network failures and latency: partitions, slow links and site failures affect availability and response times; recovery must handle partially completed operations.
4. Distributed query processing and optimization: deciding where to execute and how much data to ship between sites is complex and costly.
5. Security: more sites and network traffic mean a larger attack surface; data must be encrypted in transit and access controlled at every site.
6. Data fragmentation and allocation design: deciding how to partition and place data for performance.
7. Administration complexity: backups, upgrades, monitoring and schema changes across heterogeneous sites; higher cost and skills required.
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• At least four valid challenges, each briefly explained — 1.5 marks each (named only: 0.5).
• Accept: consistency/replication, distributed transactions/2PC/concurrency, network failures/latency/availability, query optimization, security, fragmentation/allocation, deadlocks, administration/cost, heterogeneity.
hint: Data lives on many sites connected by a network. What gets harder: keeping copies in step, transactions, failures, queries, security?

body: Explain the abstract view of data.
answer:
The abstract view of data means the DBMS hides the complex details of how data is physically stored and maintained, and presents users with a simplified view of only what they need.

• Users and programmers work with logical structures (tables, records, relationships) rather than files, blocks, pointers and indexes on disk.
• Different users can be given different views of the same database.
• This is achieved through levels of abstraction (physical, logical/conceptual, view/external), which supports data independence — the storage or logical structure can change without changing applications.
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• Hiding storage/implementation complexity from users — 1 mark.
• Presenting a simplified/relevant view (users see only what they need) — 1 mark.
• Link to levels of abstraction and/or data independence — 1 mark.
hint: Abstraction means hiding detail. What does a DBMS hide from users about how data is stored?

body: State and explain any two levels of data abstraction.
answer:
Any two of:

1. Physical (internal) level — the lowest level; describes how data is actually stored: files, blocks, record layouts, indexes, hashing, compression. Mainly the concern of the DBMS and DBA.

2. Logical (conceptual) level — describes what data is stored and the relationships among it: entities, attributes, tables, data types, constraints, for the whole database, without storage details. Used by DBAs and designers.

3. View (external) level — the highest level; describes only the part of the database relevant to a particular user or application, e.g. a student portal sees only courses and grades while the bursar sees fees. Simplifies use and improves security.
explanation:
Marking guide (4 marks):
• Each of two correctly named levels with a correct explanation — 2 marks each (name 0.5, explanation 1.5).
hint: There are three levels, from disk to user: physical, logical (conceptual), view (external).

body:
A transaction is a sequence of database operations that access the database.

What is a database transaction?
answer:
A database transaction is a logical unit of work made up of one or more database operations (reads and writes such as SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) that must be executed as a single, indivisible unit: either all of them succeed and are committed, or none take effect (rolled back).

It moves the database from one consistent state to another. Example: transferring GH₵100 — debit account A and credit account B; if the credit fails, the debit must be undone.

Transactions begin (BEGIN/START TRANSACTION) and end with COMMIT or ROLLBACK, and are expected to satisfy the ACID properties.
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• A unit of work / sequence of operations treated as one — 1 mark.
• All-or-nothing: commit or rollback; consistent state to consistent state — 1 mark.
• Example or mention of COMMIT/ROLLBACK/ACID — 1 mark.
hint: Think of a bank transfer: debit one account, credit another. What must be true of the whole group of steps?

body: List and describe the properties that all database transactions should display.
answer:
The ACID properties:

1. Atomicity — "all or nothing". All operations in a transaction complete successfully, or none do; if any step fails the whole transaction is rolled back. Example: in a funds transfer, the debit is undone if the credit fails. Managed by the recovery system (logs/undo).

2. Consistency — a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another, preserving all integrity rules (constraints, keys, triggers, business rules). Example: total money in the bank is unchanged by a transfer.

3. Isolation — concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other; intermediate results of one transaction are not visible to others, so the outcome is as if they ran one after another (serializability). Enforced by concurrency control (locks, MVCC, isolation levels).

4. Durability — once a transaction commits, its changes are permanent and survive system crashes or power failures. Ensured by write-ahead logs, checkpoints and backups.
explanation:
Marking guide (10 marks):
• Atomicity named and described — 2.5 marks.
• Consistency named and described — 2.5 marks.
• Isolation named and described — 2.5 marks.
• Durability named and described — 2.5 marks.
• A property named without description earns about 0.5. Examples strengthen answers. (The 2024/25 paper awarded 8 marks for this question; scale is the same.)
hint: Four letters: A, C, I, D.

body: List and explain TWO (2) techniques for backup in the database system.
answer:
Any two of:

1. Full backup — a complete copy of the entire database at a point in time. Simplest and fastest to restore, but takes the most time and storage.

2. Incremental backup — copies only data changed since the last backup of any type. Fast and small, but restoring needs the last full backup plus every incremental in order.

3. Differential backup — copies all changes since the last full backup. Larger than incremental, but restore needs only the full backup plus the latest differential.

4. Transaction log backup / point-in-time recovery — backs up the transaction log so the database can be restored to a precise moment.

5. Mirroring/replication or snapshots — continuously maintained copies on another server or storage snapshots for fast recovery.

Also: hot (online) vs cold (offline) backups; logical (SQL dump) vs physical (file copy) backups.
explanation:
Marking guide (4 marks):
• Each of two valid techniques named and explained — 2 marks each.
hint: Compare copying everything vs copying only what changed.

TRUNCATE TABLE LeagueTable

What will the code above do? Show the instance.
answer:
TRUNCATE TABLE LeagueTable removes ALL rows from LeagueTable at once, but keeps the table itself — its structure (columns, data types), constraints and indexes remain, so it can be used again.

Instance after execution: the table still exists with its column headings but has zero rows (an empty table), e.g. a SELECT * FROM LeagueTable returns only the headings and "0 rows".

Characteristics: it is a DDL command; it is faster than DELETE because it deallocates data pages rather than deleting row by row; it cannot have a WHERE clause; it does not fire row DELETE triggers; it usually resets identity/auto-increment counters; and in many DBMSs it cannot easily be rolled back.

• Removes all rows/records — 1 mark.
• Table structure remains (not dropped) — 1 mark.
• Instance shown/described as an empty table with its columns, or valid additional detail (no WHERE, faster than DELETE, resets identity) — 1 mark.

body: Differentiate between a two-tier architecture and a three-tier architecture.
answer:
Two-tier (client–server) architecture:
• The client application talks directly to the database server.
• The presentation and business logic run on the client; the database server stores and manages data.
• Example: a desktop app connecting straight to MySQL over ODBC/JDBC.
• Simple and fast for small numbers of users, but harder to scale, less secure (clients hold DB credentials) and every client must be updated when logic changes.

Three-tier architecture:
• Adds a middle (application) tier between client and database: presentation tier (browser/UI) → application/business-logic tier (web/app server) → data tier (database server).
• Clients never access the database directly.
• Example: a web application — browser, PHP/Node/Java server, database.
• More scalable, secure and maintainable: logic is centralised, tiers can be scaled and updated independently; but more complex and with extra network hops.
explanation:
Marking guide (4 marks):
• Two-tier correctly described (client communicates directly with DB server; logic on client) — 1.5 marks.
• Three-tier correctly described (presentation, application/business logic, data tiers) — 1.5 marks.
• At least one valid contrast (scalability, security, maintenance, performance) or examples — 1 mark.
hint: Count the layers between the user's screen and the database. Where does the business logic live?

body: Differentiate between Normalization and Data Dictionary.
answer:
Normalization is a database design process of organising tables and their attributes to reduce data redundancy and avoid update, insertion and deletion anomalies. It decomposes tables according to normal forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF) based on functional dependencies, e.g. splitting customer details out of an orders table.

A Data Dictionary (system catalog) is a centralised repository of metadata — "data about data". It describes the database's objects: table and column names, data types, sizes, constraints, keys, relationships, indexes, views, users and privileges. The DBMS and DBAs use it to manage and document the database.

Difference: normalization is an activity that shapes the structure of the data; the data dictionary is a store that records and describes that structure.
explanation:
Marking guide (4 marks):
• Normalization correctly explained (process, reduces redundancy/anomalies, normal forms) — 2 marks.
• Data dictionary correctly explained (metadata repository describing tables, columns, types, constraints) — 2 marks.
hint: One is a design process; the other is a catalogue that describes the database.

body: Explain the following database term: Relation
answer: A relation is a two-dimensional table in the relational model, made up of rows (tuples) and columns (attributes), with a name and a defined schema. Each row is unique, each column has a unique name and a domain of values, values are atomic, and the order of rows and columns does not matter. Example: a STUDENT relation with attributes StudentNo, Name, Programme.
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• A table of rows and columns in the relational model — 1 mark.
• Properties (unique rows, atomic values, named attributes) or example — 1 mark.
hint: In the relational model, what is a table formally called?

body: Explain the following database term: Tuple
answer: A tuple is a single row (record) in a relation (table). It holds one value for each attribute and represents one instance of the entity, e.g. (0103, 'Harriet', 'O'Casey') is one tuple in a Student table. Each tuple in a relation must be unique, usually identified by the primary key. The number of tuples is the relation's cardinality.
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• A row/record in a relation — 1 mark.
• Explanation or example (one entity instance, unique, set of attribute values) — 1 mark.
hint: It's one of these in a table.

body: Explain the following database term: Field
answer: A field is a single column (attribute) in a table, holding one kind of data about the entity, with a name and data type, e.g. LastName VARCHAR(50) or DateOfBirth DATE. In a single record, the field holds one data value — the intersection of a row and a column. The number of fields is the relation's degree.
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• A column/attribute holding one item of data — 1 mark.
• Explanation or example (name, data type, value in a record) — 1 mark.
hint: Rows are records; what are the columns?

body: What is the difference between DML and DDL?
answer:
DDL (Data Definition Language) defines and changes the structure (schema) of database objects: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME. Its changes are usually auto-committed and affect tables, indexes, views, etc.

DML (Data Manipulation Language) works with the data stored inside those objects: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE (and MERGE). DML changes can be committed or rolled back within a transaction.

Example: CREATE TABLE Students (...) is DDL; INSERT INTO Students VALUES (...) is DML.
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• DDL defines/modifies structure with examples — 1.5 marks.
• DML manipulates/retrieves data with examples — 1.5 marks.
hint: One changes the data; the other changes the structure that holds it.

body: List four DML commands and state their functions.
answer:
• SELECT — retrieves (queries) data from one or more tables.
• INSERT — adds new rows to a table.
• UPDATE — modifies existing rows.
• DELETE — removes rows from a table.
(MERGE — inserts or updates in one statement — is also acceptable.)
explanation:

• 0.5 marks for each of four correct DML commands with their function.
hint: Read, add, change, remove.

body: What is the purpose of the IN operator?
answer:
The IN operator tests whether a value matches any value in a list or in the result of a subquery, in a WHERE clause. It is shorthand for multiple OR conditions.

Example: SELECT * FROM Students WHERE State IN ('KY', 'CO', 'CA');
is the same as State = 'KY' OR State = 'CO' OR State = 'CA'.
With a subquery: WHERE CourseNo IN (SELECT CourseNo FROM Courses WHERE CreditHours = 3). NOT IN excludes the values.
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• Checks a value against a list/subquery (shorthand for multiple ORs) — 1 mark.
• Correct example — 1 mark.
hint: A shorter way of writing several OR conditions.

body: How does SQL handle NULL values in conditions?
answer:
• NULL represents a missing or unknown value; it is not zero or an empty string.
• Any comparison with NULL using =, <>, <, > evaluates to UNKNOWN (three-valued logic: TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN), and WHERE only keeps rows where the condition is TRUE. So WHERE Phone = NULL returns no rows — even rows whose Phone is NULL.
• You must use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL: WHERE Phone IS NULL.
• NOT IN with a list containing NULL returns no rows; aggregate functions (SUM, AVG, COUNT(column)) ignore NULLs, while COUNT(*) counts all rows.
• Functions like COALESCE(Phone, 'N/A') or IFNULL/ISNULL replace NULLs with a default.

• Comparisons with NULL yield unknown / = NULL doesn't work — 1 mark.
• Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL — 1 mark.
• Any further correct point (aggregates ignore NULL, COALESCE/IFNULL, three-valued logic, NOT IN pitfall) — 1 mark.
hint: NULL means unknown. Is unknown equal to anything — even another unknown?

SELECT StudentNo, COUNT(CourseNo) AS Courses
FROM Enrollments
GROUP BY StudentNo
HAVING COUNT(CourseNo) > 2;

FROM Students s JOIN Enrollments e ON e.StudentNo = s.StudentNo
GROUP BY s.StudentNo, s.FirstName, s.LastName
HAVING COUNT(*) > 2;

FROM Enrollments e
JOIN Students s ON s.StudentNo = e.StudentNo

or use RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) = 1, or LIMIT 1 / TOP 1.

body: What is the purpose of the ORDER BY clause?
answer:
ORDER BY sorts the rows in a query's result set by one or more columns or expressions, in ascending (ASC, the default) or descending (DESC) order. Without it, SQL does not guarantee any row order.

Example: SELECT * FROM Products ORDER BY Category ASC, Price DESC; — sorts by category, then by price from highest to lowest within each category.
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• Sorts the result set by column(s) — 1 mark.
• ASC/DESC and/or example — 1 mark.
hint: It doesn't change which rows you get — only how they're arranged.

body: Why is GROUP BY used with aggregate functions?
answer:
Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) summarise many rows into one value. On their own they summarise the whole table.

GROUP BY divides the rows into groups that share the same value(s) in the grouping column(s), and the aggregate is then calculated separately for each group — producing one summary row per group. Example: SELECT State, COUNT(*) FROM Students GROUP BY State; gives the number of students in each state rather than one overall total.

Rules: every non-aggregated column in the SELECT list must appear in GROUP BY; to filter groups by an aggregate use HAVING (e.g. HAVING COUNT(*) > 2), since WHERE filters rows before grouping.

hint: Without GROUP BY, SUM gives one number for the whole table. What if you want one number per category?

body: What is the difference between DELETE and TRUNCATE?
answer:
DELETE:
• DML command; removes rows one at a time and can use a WHERE clause to remove only some rows.
• Each deleted row is logged; slower on large tables.
• Fires DELETE triggers; can be rolled back within a transaction.
• Does not reset identity/auto-increment counters.

TRUNCATE:
• DDL command; removes ALL rows at once by deallocating data pages — no WHERE clause.
• Minimal logging; much faster.
• Does not fire row triggers; usually resets identity counters; cannot be rolled back in many DBMSs (e.g. MySQL, Oracle).
